newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr learns to live with lower rates.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr learns to live with lower rates.

text.p: The Australian dollar regained some poise through a calmer Thursday session as Japanese buying suggested yesterday's surprise rate cut had not completely ruined the currency's appeal.
Volumes were light but traders were impressed that heavy selling had been absorbed offshore while keeping US$0.7890 support intact, and felt a bounce to US$0.7950 was possible.

Sentiment was also shored by a firmer than expected set of labour data for November, which at least showed the economy was not in the sort of tailspin that would need further, immediate remedial action from monetary policy.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local dollar was trying to put its life back together at US$0.7924/29 having nudged up from a US$0.7889 low and US$0.7915/20 late here Wednesday.
That was still well down on the US$0.8020 level held before yesterday's shock rate cut, however, and traders reported stiff offers all the way up to US$0.7950 chart resistance.

On the crosses it took an early hit when the yen was lifted by a Japanese newspaper report quoting a Bank of Japan official saying the bank might consider a rate hike next spring. The dollar dipped as deep as 88.83 yen but bounced when another BOJ official said the comments had been quoted rather wrongly.
The latter official also emphasised the priority for the BOJ was to address the risk of the economy not being strong enough, which analysts took as shorthand for a steady monetary policy.
That helped the dollar back up to 89.33/43 yen but it remained short of Wednesday's late 89.60/70.
In trade weighted terms it was unchanged at 58.8.

The nervousness over BOJ policy still saw JGB yields edge higher in response, an unwelcome development for dollar bulls since the interest premium offered by A$ assets had narrowed sharply in the wake of the Reserve Bank's 0.5 point cut in offical cash rates to 6.0 percent.
In particular, the easing had shrunk the gap between domestic and U.S. yields on the 2-3 year part of the curve which Japanese investors favoured most.
This raised concerns they might turn more to dual currency samurai bonds denominated in U.S. dollars and away from the yen/A$ issues which have led the boom in this sector all year.
Dealers noted the last A$ issue had been on December 3, disappointing expectations that the winter bonus season in Japan would lead to a rush of fresh demand.
And the local dollar still faced the risk of yet another policy easing at home.
The RBA's statement on its cut showed it was relaxed on the inflation outlook and keen to let the economy run faster to reduce stubbornly high unemployment rates.

Today's jobs data gave only cold comfort on this front despite a 24,400 rise in employment which topped market forecasts of a 10,000 gain. The unemployment rate also eased to a four month low of 8.5 percent from 8.8 in October.

John Peters, a senior economist at Westpac, noted only 61,000 jobs had been created over the year so far and the annual growth rate of employment was a modest 0.7 percent, far too slow to make substantial inroads into unemployment.
As long as wage claims remained well behaved, he saw scope for further largesse on the policy front next year.

"Continued weakness in employment growth, generally soft economic conditions and a further wilting in underlying prices pressures will elave the door open for another 0.5 point cut in early 1997," said Peters.
The flow of domestic data dries up almost completely from now to the new year with the only relase of note being merchandise imports for November next Wednesday.
